title: Clean Up a Unix Path
statement:
You get an absolute Unix-style file path path (it always starts with /). Return its shortest equivalent form. The rules:

  • Several slashes in a row act like one slash.
  • . means the current folder and can be dropped.
  • .. means the parent folder. At the root, .. stays at the root.
  • Any other name is an ordinary folder name, including names made only of dots such as ....

The result starts with a single /, separates names with single slashes, contains no . or .. parts, and does not end with a slash unless it is just /.

examples.why: The double slash collapses, "." disappears, and the trailing slash is dropped.
Two ".." climb back to the root; the third one has nowhere higher to go and is ignored.
"..." is a real folder name, not a command. The final ".." only leaves x.

hints: Split the path on '/' and look at the pieces one by one. Which pieces can you simply ignore?
Each folder name goes one level deeper; each '..' undoes the most recent level. Which structure undoes the most recent thing?
Push names onto a stack, pop on '..' (if the stack is not empty), skip '' and '.', then join the stack with '/' behind a leading '/'.

explain.intuition:
Reading a path left to right is like walking through folders. A name steps in, .. steps back out of the folder you entered most recently. "Undo the latest step" is exactly what a stack does.

After splitting on /, the empty pieces (from double or trailing slashes) and the . pieces change nothing. Names are pushed, .. pops if there is anything to pop, and whatever is left on the stack, bottom to top, is the clean path. This is the same thing a browser does when it resolves a relative URL like ../img/logo.png.
steps: For .., pop the stack if it is not empty.
pitfalls: Treating any piece that starts with a dot as special. Only exactly . and .. are; ... and .c are names.
Popping on .. when the stack is empty, which throws or produces a path above the root.
Joining without the leading slash, or returning an empty string instead of / for the root.

solutions.title: Split and use a stack
solutions.idea: Split on '/', push names, pop on '..', ignore empty pieces and '.'.

solutions.title: Single scan without split
solutions.idea: Walk the string with an index, cut out each name between slashes yourself, and apply the same stack rules.

followups: Resolve a relative path such as "../x/./y" against a current directory given as a second argument.
Add symbolic links: some names map to other absolute paths. How do you avoid looping forever?
